card.thesis: This engine has no cross-symbol operator -- entry and exit are evaluated per instrument against that instrument's own bars only -- so 'rotation' here is produced entirely by the universe, the fixed fill order, and a 3-of-6 slot cap, not by any rule that compares one symbol to another. What the card does: apply one absolute filter (close above its own 100-day average, RSI(14) between 50 and 75 -- an established but not extended move) identically across six instruments split into two economically opposed legs: a defensive-equity leg (XLP staples, XLU utilities, XLV health care -- the three lowest-beta S&P sectors) and an energy/commodity reflation leg (XLE energy, DBC broad commodities, USO crude oil). Each leg is only ever held when its own trend is intact; the same filter drops a name the moment its trend breaks, with no view on what should happen next. I deliberately excluded Treasuries and gold from this universe -- the classic disinflation hedge -- because that basket (TLT/IEF/GLD/LQD) is already the field's `c14-riskmanaged-wide` card; building the same basket again under a different label would be one hypothesis wearing two names, which is exactly the redundancy Benjamini-Hochberg correction penalizes every other card for. This card instead answers a different question: which side of the value/defensive-versus-growth axis is actually confirmed in trend right now, given no ability to compare the two sides directly, only to filter each independently. The other side of these trades: momentum capital that stays concentrated in the AI/growth complex through a rotation because that is its mandate, not because it disagrees about the rotation; cross-asset traders who fade an energy or commodity breakout as 'a dead trade' and get run over by a multi-month reflation move (their mirror-image mistake is fading a defensive-sector rally as 'boring' and missing a growth-scare rotation); and momentum/CTA flow on the other side of whichever leg is currently exiting, since a slow, rule-following trend-break here is a late seller relative to a discretionary desk. I measured, through 2026-02-13: trailing 252-session correlation of each name's daily return to QQQ (used as a proxy for the AI/growth-momentum complex both B-momentum and C-trend trade) -- XLP 0.188, USO 0.270, DBC 0.342, XLU 0.397, XLV 0.430, XLE 0.509 -- mean 0.356, below the 0.57 the round's own brief measures between B-momentum and C-trend, though not as low as c14's near-zero figure, because equity-sector and energy exposure still carries real beta to broad risk sentiment that a pure bond/gold book does not. Breadth: on the 4,994 sessions since 2006-04-09 (all six symbols have data) where the entry filter is computable, a median of 3 of 6 and a mean of 2.78 of 6 qualify simultaneously; at least 3 qualify on 56.4% of sessions, so a 3-slot cap is a real, regularly binding constraint rather than a formality. When more than 3 qualify on the same session, the broker fills in the order below -- ascending by the same trailing correlation-to-QQQ measured above, so the names this round's own combined-book scoring cares most about (the ones least correlated to the incumbents) get filled first when a choice must be made. I am not claiming this ordering is itself a source of edge: the programme's own sensitivity test moved one card's three-year return across a 53.9-point spread (sigma 21.2) purely from re-ordering an identical universe, so any single-window margin this produces could be entirely inside that noise band, and I say so rather than dress an arbitrary-but-reasoned tiebreak up as a finding. None of these six names is selected because it is an S&P 500 or Nasdaq-100 constituent, and none is a single-stock pick at all -- five are diversified sector or commodity ETF baskets and one (USO) tracks a single physical commodity future; the selection logic is asset-class role and measured correlation to the AI-momentum complex, not survivorship-adjacent index membership, so this card does not inherit the universe_knowable_from gate. I do flag honestly that the sector SPDRs' own internal holdings rebalance to track the present-day S&P 500's sector composition, which is a much weaker and indirect version of the same effect. Sized well under the book: 3 slots at 15% is a 45% maximum commitment, against the A-family's ~90% nominal (and ~0.47-0.49 realised) capital exposure that this discipline was retired for; a naive occupancy proxy (mean of min(qualifying,3) times 0.15 across the same history) comes to roughly 0.32, meaningfully below the A family's realised figure by construction, not by luck. What this does that passively holding the same six names would not: a static equal-weight holding of XLP/XLU/XLV/XLE/DBC/USO would have been long the energy/commodity leg all the way into its oil-2014 collapse and would have owned whichever leg is currently breaking down at all times; this card only ever holds a name while its own trend is intact, exits it on a trend break or a 10% stop (whichever comes first against the next session's open, since fills and stops both act on lagging prices, not the intraday low), and caps how much of the book any single regime call can consume. That is discipline over exposure, not prediction of direction -- it will lag every turn by design, and I say what that costs in the falsification section of the accompanying memo.
card.entry: close > sma(100) and rsi(14) > 50 and rsi(14) < 75

card.thesis: Mechanism: RSI(2) below 10 while price still sits above its 200-day SMA identifies a 1-3 day, statistically extreme downside spike inside an intact long-term uptrend -- forced or panicked short-horizon selling (stop-loss triggers, single-stock margin calls, index-fund rebalancing flow, overreaction to a headline) in a name whose underlying demand (consumer staples, branded pharma, integrated energy) has no reason to have changed in 48 hours. The 200-day filter is the same 'nothing structural has broken' proxy c01-meanrev used; the entry indicator is deliberately much shorter and much stricter than c01's bb_lower(20,2) so it fires on genuine short-horizon panic rather than on any garden-variety pullback, and it targets a faster, shallower bounce rather than a full band-width reversion. The counterparty is whoever sold into that 1-3 day spike without repricing fundamentals -- forced sellers, momentum-following short-term traders extending a move, or algorithmic stop cascades. My exit (close back above the 5-day SMA) sells into the snapback while it is still fresh, rather than waiting for a slower 20-day mean the position may never reach. Pre-registered failure regime: a fast, deep, *sustained* decline where the 200-day SMA has not yet turned down -- the entry keeps re-firing on 'dips' that are actually the first third of a much bigger leg down (2008's Sep-Oct acceleration is the closest historical analogue among this round's windows), and the 5-day-SMA exit and 10-day time stop do not arrive before the position is stopped out, repeatedly, until the 200-day average finally rolls over.

This engine cannot express relative strength: entry and exit are evaluated per symbol against that symbol's own bars, with no cross-sectional comparison, so there is no way to buy 'the strongest semiconductor name' or trade a spread. What this card actually does is apply one absolute condition -- close above its own 50-day average with RSI(14) between 55 and 80, i.e. a confirmed, non-extreme uptrend -- identically to a 9-name cyclical-semiconductor universe (NVDA AMD MU INTC MRVL AVGO TSM QCOM SOXX), and cap concurrent holdings at 3 of 9. That cap is the only 'rotation' logic available: the mechanism is that semiconductor demand and AI-capex cycles tend to move the whole group together and to persist for quarters rather than days, so entering only into names already confirmed in trend, and exiting on trend break or momentum fade, should keep capital on the right side of the cycle more often than not, while the cap prevents any single session from committing to more than 3 names at once. I measured pairwise daily-return correlation across these 9 names over the trailing ~253 sessions through 2026-02-13: mean 0.589, range 0.286 (INTC vs AVGO) to 0.824 (SOXX vs TSM). That is high -- this is a concentrated sector bet dressed as a 3-of-9 rotation, not a diversified basket, and I am not pretending otherwise. It is not a coin-flip between one name and nothing, though: breadth genuinely varies session to session under the proposed filter (median 4 of 9 names qualifying; at least 4 qualify on 50.6% of sessions, at least 6 on 21.3%), so the cap binds and actually forces a choice often enough to matter. When more than 3 names qualify on the same session, the broker fills entries in the fixed order the universe list is written -- alphabetical here -- not by any measure of relative strength, momentum magnitude, or liquidity. That is an arbitrary tiebreak, not a 'buy the leader' mechanism, and the card cannot do better than that. On the other side of these trades: momentum/trend traders who initiated the move earlier and are already positioned before this rule confirms it; mean-reversion sellers who fade strength too early inside a still-intact uptrend and get run over; and dip-buyers in choppy or declining regimes who buy bottoms this rule cannot see coming and will instead get chopped by.
card.entry: close > sma(50) and rsi(14) > 55 and rsi(14) < 80

card.thesis: Institutional flow into AI/cloud-infrastructure leaders re-rates them in slow, multi-week waves, not single days: a fund building a position over weeks pushes the medium-term average through the long-term one, and that crossover is a public, mechanical signal other trend-following capital reacts to next, extending the move further than any one participant intended. On the design-window history of these 12 names, once close > sma(200) is already established and ema(20) crosses above ema(50) -- a fresh acceleration inside a standing uptrend, not a bottom-pick -- the resulting move has a median duration of roughly 3-4 weeks and stretches past two months at the 75th percentile (NVDA's longest such run reached 256 sessions, MSFT's 169, TSM's 189). The other side of this trade is whoever sells into that strength: value-discipline holders trimming into a re-rate, and short sellers pressing a name that 'already ran too far' -- both wrong, on average, while the wave is still building. I tested a fixed take-profit and a fast rule exit against simply riding the position to a stop or a genuine trend break, on this same entry: capping gains at 8-30% cut mean per-signal return to 2-9%, and a fast 20-day-EMA exit (even with a 3-day confirmation filter) cut it to 3-5% and win rate to 42-49% by whipsawing out of live trends on ordinary pullbacks. Letting the position run to a stop, a 200-day trend-break, or a 180-day backstop produced roughly triple the aggregate return of either capped variant, at the cost of a median trade near breakeven-to-slightly-negative -- this strategy's edge is concentrated in a minority of large winners, which is exactly what a take-profit would have amputated. It is deliberately not diversified across volatility regimes: the universe was chosen so one stop and one position size fit all 12 names reasonably rather than being tuned to any single one.
card.entry: ema(20) crosses_above ema(50) and close > sma(200)

card.thesis: AI-capex-cycle names re-rate on multi-quarter earnings-revision cycles, not single days: a data-center or cloud demand cycle shows up as a sequence of beat-and-raise quarters that institutional allocators scale into over months, not one print. That flow creates serial correlation in price that a same-day oscillator cannot see. The other side of the trade is investors who sell into strength too early, anchored to a pre-cycle 'fair value', and investors who panic-sell the first pullback inside an intact uptrend, mistaking noise for reversal -- both hand the rest of the move to a slower, rule-following holder. I measured this rather than assuming it: on this universe's last ~1500 sessions (~6y) through 2026-02-13, a close>sma(200) regime filter plus a 20/50-EMA crossover trigger produced 77 trades at 49.4% win rate, but average winners (+29.6%) were 4.1x average losers (-7.3%), and winning trades were held a median of 118 days vs 16 for losers -- the classic trend signature of a system that is right less than half the time and still profitable because it cuts losses fast and lets the rest run. The chop problem is real and I confronted it directly: the same golden-cross setup on this universe's smaller, more speculative names (IREN, OKLO, APLD, BE, KORU) produced negative average 60-day forward returns after the signal fired -- those names were excluded from the universe below specifically because the measured data showed the entries do not sustain here, not because of a prior. Within the chosen universe, widening the stop from 8% to 12% cut stop-outs from 12/77 (16%) to 7/77 (9%) while barely moving mean trade return (0.093->0.093), meaning most of the discarded stop-outs at the tighter level were noise, not real breakdowns -- direct evidence the wider stop survives chop without giving back the move. The regime filter (sma200) plus a medium-term trigger (ema20/50, not raw ema50/200) was chosen over a textbook dual-moving-average cross because it produces materially fewer whipsaw entries on this universe's large, liquid AI/semi/software names, at the cost of entering somewhat later into each trend.
card.entry: close > sma(200) and ema(20) crosses_above ema(50)

card.display_name: H - Trend, cross-asset: lowest drawdown of the trend family
card.thesis: Round 1 forced this discipline into one sector; round 2 lets me test its central weakness directly -- trend following's worst outcome is not a bad trade, it is every position turning at once, which is a correlation problem before it is a signal problem. I measured correlation rather than assumed it. Trailing 2y (504-session) daily-return correlation across my round-1 universe (NVDA AVGO TSM ORCL SOXX NFLX MU META QCOM) averages 0.501 pairwise (median 0.468, range 0.219-0.800) through 2026-02-13 -- nine names sharing one regime. The round-2 roster this card actually trades (NVDA MU GDX EWZ FXI INDA DBC) averages 0.274 pairwise over the same window, a ~45% reduction, with every pair outside the NVDA/MU core below 0.39 and GDX the most decoupled name in the set (0.16-0.22 vs NVDA/MU). But correlation alone is not sufficient, and I tested that too: I ran the identical unscaled rule (close>sma(200) & ema(20)-crosses-above-ema(50) entry, ema(20)-crosses-below-ema(50) exit, 12% stop, 120-day time stop -- same parameters as my round-1 card, same trailing ~1500-session/6y design methodology) on every 'obvious diversifier' round 2 exposes. Bonds (TLT, mean trade return -1.6% over 5 trades), utilities (XLU, -0.5% over 18 trades), regional banks (KRE, -0.8%), biotech (XBI, -0.2%), copper (CPER, -1.1%) and defence (ITA, +2.2% mean but only 28.6% win rate, and 0.53 correlated to the semis sleeve -- a worse diversifier than gold despite the label) all showed flat-to-negative or too-thin edge under this exact rule to earn a slot: including them would not have reduced correlated drawdown, it would have parked capital in dead-or-negative-expectancy positions that still occasionally fire a badly-timed entry. Gold miners (GDX) were the standout: 4 trades in 6y, 75% win rate, +20.9% mean trade return, lowest correlation to the core of anything tested. Brazil (EWZ, +2.1% mean trade, 0.23-0.30 corr), China (FXI, +2.8%, 0.24-0.31 corr), India (INDA, +4.5%, 0.21-0.26 corr, only 0.07 correlated to DBC) and broad commodities (DBC, +5.5%, 0.07-0.39 corr) all cleared a lower but genuinely positive bar and are the five diversifying sleeves in this universe. NVDA and MU stay as the trend engine because that is where the measured edge is largest -- +17.3% and +20.6% mean trade return respectively in the same 6y window, against +12.7% averaged across all nine round-1 names and +9.7% averaged across this seven-name diversified book. The mechanism is unchanged from round 1: gradual institutional flow into a confirmed uptrend, plus both premature profit-taking and panicked pullback-selling handing the rest of a move to a slower, rule-following holder -- but now spread across sleeves whose macro drivers are structurally different (US AI capex cycle, gold's real-rate/dollar cycle, EM equity flows, broad commodity demand), so a single regime turning cannot take out the whole book the way it structurally can in a one-sector universe. This is a real trade-off, not a free lunch: the diversified book's measured per-trade expectancy (9.7%) is lower than the concentrated book's (12.7%) on this identical rule and sample -- I am spending some expected return to buy a reduction in simultaneous-drawdown risk, and round 1 is the direct comparison for whether that trade was worth it. Realised 2y annualised volatility on this universe ranges from INDA (14.1%) to MU (60.0%), a 4.3x spread wider than round 1's uniformly high-vol semis cluster, exactly as the brief warned. I did not rescale the single 12% stop because the engine cannot: it is proportionately tight on NVDA/MU (12.5%-25% measured stop-hit rate in the design window) and proportionately loose on INDA/DBC/EWZ/FXI (0% measured stop-hit rate over the same window) -- I am stating that mismatch rather than pretending a single number fits both a 60%-vol stock and a 14%-vol commodity ETF equally well.
card.entry: close > sma(200) and ema(20) crosses_above ema(50)

card.thesis: Sector SPDRs oscillate around a short-term fair-value anchor because most of their daily volume comes from liquidity providers, index rebalancers and short-horizon momentum traders rather than investors repricing fundamentals -- fundamentals for a nine-sector basket do not change materially week to week. When RSI(14) drops below 30 AND the close is also below the 20-day, 2-stddev Bollinger lower band, two independent measures (momentum exhaustion and a statistically stretched price relative to recent volatility) agree that the move has overshot. The other side of that trade is forced or reflexive selling that does not price on fair value -- stop-loss cascades, volatility-targeting deleveraging, tax-loss and rebalancing flows -- and it does not persist once the flow clears, which is why we exit on the close reclaiming the 20-day mean rather than holding for a trend. This mechanism needs mean reversion to actually be the dominant force, which is true in a range-bound market and false in a fast one-directional break, where 'oversold' does not mean 'done falling' and the entry buys into a crash that keeps crashing. We measured this directly: in chop-2015 the rule produced 23 trades averaging +2.42% (70% win rate); in chop-2011, 25 trades averaging +0.93% (72% win rate). In covid the same rule, unchanged, produced 18 trades averaging -6.53% with a 17% win rate and 15 of 18 exits were stops -- see the memo for the full comparison and the sensitivity check confirming this split is not an artifact of the specific thresholds chosen.

In a systemic equity selloff capital does not vanish, it rotates: institutional and retail sellers de-risk out of equities into US duration (Treasuries) and, in uncertainty-driven episodes, into gold. That rotation shows up first as a volatility breakout in the receiving instrument's own price -- a close pushing above its 20-day Bollinger upper band -- because a sudden, forced buying wave widens the band and breaks it before any slower moving-average filter would confirm a trend. The other side of that trade is whoever is still willing to sell duration or gold at the pre-rotation price: in ordinary markets TLT and GLD are unremarkable, low-conviction holdings that drift on yield and macro views with no connection to equity risk, so a band breakout in either is a cheap, low-information signal most of the time and costs a string of small whipsaw losses. It becomes a strong, well-paid signal exactly when equity holders are forced, non-price-sensitive sellers of risk and buyers of safety, because that is the one condition under which the other side of a TLT/GLD trade is not a considered view but a stampede. This card holds TLT and GLD outright -- real capital, real price risk, sized at 15% of starting equity per slot -- so its payoff comes from a position actually carried through the dislocation, not from sitting out of SPY while it falls; roughly 85% of the book is uninvested cash at any time, which this engine scores as free but which a real book would have to fund, invest, or forgo yield on. I expect this card's numerically worst window to be bull-2024: a strong, low-volatility equity year gives TLT and GLD no rotation to catch, so the entry still fires on ordinary volatility noise, whipsaws against sma(20), and pays its premium with nothing to show for it. Separately, and worth flagging even though it is not the predicted worst *number*: bear-2022 is the window where the underlying mechanism itself fails, not just goes unpaid -- 2022 was a rate-hike-driven decline that hurt equities and duration together, so there was no flight-to-quality rotation into TLT to catch, and the card's raw return there is a real loss (the low-exposure denominator in the scoring only cushions how that loss compares to the benchmark, it does not mean the trade worked).

A confirmed swing-high breakout marks the point where a market has absorbed all the supply that capped it at the old pivot -- the resting sellers at that level have been cleared, so the next marginal buyer transacts at a new equilibrium with less overhead resistance above. The counterparty giving up the trade is the anchoring seller who priced the old high as fair value and is now underwater on that anchor; they cover or step aside rather than average down into a level that just failed to hold. This mechanism is not equity-specific -- it is a statement about order-book supply and anchoring bias, so it should recur in any liquid, exchange-traded, trend-capable market: government bonds, gold, investment-grade credit, not just stock indices. Round 1's breakout card tested that claim with nine US sector ETFs, which are nine expressions of the same equity-beta trend and were later measured near 0.58 mean pairwise correlation -- one bet in nine costumes, which is why its win rate moved by window and not by symbol within a window. This card tests the mechanism across four assets chosen specifically because their return drivers differ (equity risk premium, interest-rate duration, monetary/safe-haven demand, investment-grade credit spread), and reports the measured correlation matrix rather than asserting diversification. The trend filter (price above its 200-day average) is there to avoid buying a breakout that is really a dead-cat bounce inside a larger downtrend; it also means the strategy is structurally absent during the worst of a fast crash, which is arithmetic, not risk management, and is declared as such rather than claimed as skill.
card.entry: close crosses_above swing_high(20) and close > sma(200)

card.display_name: C14 - Risk-managed: flight-to-quality basket, built for the worst window
card.thesis: This card is not trying to top the median-return table. It is designed for the worst-window column of the Pareto frontier: when equities are in genuine distress, capital does not evaporate, it moves -- into long and intermediate Treasuries, into gold, and to a lesser extent into investment-grade credit -- because those are the instruments large pools of capital are mandated or incentivised to hold when risk appetite collapses (pension and insurance duration-matching flows, safe-haven gold demand, and credit's senior claim relative to equity). The other side of every one of my trades is whoever is still selling those instruments into the flight, or the momentum/carry trader whose short-duration or short-vol position gets forced out; I am not claiming an edge over them in normal markets, only that I am positioned to be a buyer of what they are forced to sell exactly when SPY is worst. I measured this rather than assumed it, using only data through 2026-02-13. Buy-and-hold cumulative return of my four names, TLT/IEF/GLD/LQD, against SPY over every window fully inside the design cutoff: gfc (Oct07-Mar09) TLT +25.1% IEF +20.2% GLD +23.9% LQD -6.8% vs SPY -55.2%; covid (Feb-Jun20) TLT +13.3% IEF +7.9% GLD +10.3% LQD +3.7% vs SPY -7.9%; q4-2018 TLT +4.6% IEF +3.3% GLD +5.8% LQD -1.1% vs SPY -19.3%; chop-2011 TLT +34.3% IEF +14.5% GLD +6.1% LQD +9.0% vs SPY +1.3%. Every one of those four is a case where equities were flat-to-crushed and this basket was flat-to-strongly-positive. But I also measured the counter-case rather than hide it: bear-2022 TLT -29.3% IEF -15.4% GLD -7.3% LQD -21.1% vs SPY -24.5% -- when the shock is rate hikes rather than a growth/credit scare, duration is not a hedge, it is a second source of loss, and my basket did no better than equities and TLT individually did worse. I also checked equity 'defensive sector' alternatives (XLU, XLP) before excluding them: both fell 28-42% during gfc and 11-21% during covid, worse than SPY's own covid drawdown in XLU's case -- they are equities first and defensive second, and a credit-crisis or liquidity-crisis regime takes them down with everything else, so they do not belong in a card whose whole claim is about crisis behaviour. I also checked SLV as a second precious-metal sleeve and excluded it: -22% in chop-2011, -17% in bear-2022, -5% in gfc -- an inconsistent diversifier that would have added a name without adding ballast on the exact days that matter.
card.entry: close > sma(150) and ema(10) crosses_above ema(30) and rsi(14) < 70

card.thesis: A close below the 20-day, 2-sigma Bollinger lower band, with RSI(14) under 30 and the day's true range exceeding its own 14-day ATR, is three independent confirmations of the same event: a statistically extreme, accelerating one-day dislocation, not an ordinary pullback inside a trend. In financials and energy specifically -- the two sectors whose largest single-day moves have repeatedly been forced selling rather than a revision of fundamentals (margin calls, fund redemptions, program-driven de-grossing, a headline that gets re-priced within days once it is understood) -- that kind of move tends to partially retrace over the following one to three weeks, because the sellers on the shock day are disproportionately non-economic: risk desks cutting exposure into a VaR breach, index/ETF-driven flows, and retail panic, not new information about ten years of future cash flows for JPMorgan or Exxon. The counterparty on the other side of my buy is exactly that forced seller -- someone selling because a risk limit or a margin call requires it that day, not because they have re-underwritten the business -- and the person I hand the position to on exit is whoever is chasing the bounce once the panic is visibly over. This is a volatility-discipline entry, not a dip-buy dressed up as one: the ATR-relative range condition is what is missing from a plain RSI/Bollinger mean-reversion rule, and it is what keeps the trigger anchored to days when the market is repricing fast rather than merely drifting to an oversold reading over two quiet weeks. The strategy is a genuine short-vol / mean-reversion payoff, not a convex one: it harvests a moderate, capped reversion after each shock and is capped on the downside by a stop, but a stop checked against the prior close (not the intraday low, per the engine's execution model) means a shock that is the start of a structural decline rather than a one-day panic -- oil in the second half of 2014 is the clearest historical case in this universe -- can gap through the stop before it is caught, which is this strategy's real tail risk and is stated here before any result exists, not fitted after seeing one.
card.entry: close < bb_lower(20,2) and rsi(14) < 30 and high - low > atr(14)

card.display_name: C21 - Uncorrelated: global macro trend across commodities, precious metals and EM equities
card.thesis: This card exists to be the leg of the combined book that does not move with B-momentum or C-trend, which trade the AI/semis capex cycle through NVDA/AVGO/TSM/META-type names. My universe -- DBC, USO, GDX, FXI, EWZ, SLV -- is priced by six different demand mechanisms with nothing to do with AI capex: global commodity supply/demand and inflation expectations (DBC, USO), monetary/safe-haven demand for precious metals plus mining-equity operating leverage (GDX, SLV), and two single-country equity markets whose dominant drivers are domestic policy and currency, not US tech earnings (FXI: China regulatory and property cycle; EWZ: Brazil commodity-and-political cycle). Measured over the trailing two years through 2026-02-13, daily-return correlation of each name to an equal-weighted composite of B-momentum's 12 tickers is 0.21-0.34 (DBC 0.268, USO 0.213, GDX 0.237, FXI 0.334, EWZ 0.338; SLV in the same 0.2-0.3 band) -- all well below the B-momentum/C-trend pairing this round measured at +0.57, and well below EEM (0.655), EFA (0.594) and HYG (0.563), which I tested and rejected precisely because they still smuggle in AI-heavy Taiwan/Korea tech (EEM/EFA both hold TSM-adjacent exposure) or equity risk-on credit beta (HYG). The counterparty on my trades is whoever is positioned for a US-tech-specific cycle and is surprised by an oil supply shock, a Fed tightening surprise that moves EM currencies, or a China policy shift -- none of which shows up in an NVDA earnings call. Unlike c14's TLT/IEF/GLD/LQD, which is duration-only and was flagged as idle 55 straight live sessions because close>sma(150) rejected all four correlated bond/gold names at once, this basket's six legs are only moderately correlated with each other (they are driven by oil, gold, China policy and Brazil politics separately), so over the trailing 90 sessions through cutoff at least one name was in its close>sma(100) regime on every single session (avg 4.7 of 6 names simultaneously), with zero idle days -- the diversification that keeps correlation to B-momentum low is the same diversification that keeps this card from ever going fully dark. Entry: close>sma(100) and ema(10) crosses_above ema(30) -- a faster regime filter than c14's sma(150) and no RSI overbought gate, chosen specifically to raise firing frequency rather than restrict it, since beating c14's idle-desk problem is this card's second job. Exit is the symmetric ema(10) crosses_below ema(30), backstopped by a 15% stop (matched to this basket's 14-37% annualized vol, well above bonds but below single growth stocks) and a 150-day time stop. Measured buy-and-hold evidence in the two windows built to be adversarial to a duration hedge: taper-2013, where TLT/IEF/GLD/LQD fell 0.2% to -11.7%, this basket averaged roughly flat (+0.1%, oil's own supply rally offsetting EWZ's EM sell-off); inflation-2021, where c14's basket was uniformly negative (-3.6% to -6.2%), this basket averaged roughly +6% on commodities' inflation rally offsetting weak gold miners and EM equities. Falsification: if this basket's daily correlation to B-momentum rises materially above the measured 0.2-0.35 band once trading windows include a genuine global risk-off event (all risk assets, including commodities and EM, selling off in the same session as AI names), or if the six legs stop diversifying each other's regime timing and start entering/exiting together the way c14's four did, the uncorrelated-leg thesis is wrong, not just underperforming.
card.entry: close > sma(100) and ema(10) crosses_above ema(30)
